- Overestimate prices in bullish sentiment periods; reduce forecast highs when sentiment is strong and recent prices are rising.
- Underestimate prices in bearish sentiment periods; raise forecast lows when sentiment is negative and recent prices are falling.
- Avoid over-optimistic spikes after recent price increases; cap forecast peaks at 10–15% below true peak if sentiment is positive but recent momentum is weak.
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed, favor mean-reversion bias: forecast mid-range of recent 5–7-day average, not extreme highs/lows.
- Lagged price movements (e.g., 3–5 day delays) often over-predict short-term momentum; adjust forecasts to reflect 1–2 day lag in price acceleration.
- If sentiment is rising but price is flat or declining, reduce forecast slope; sentiment may be over-optimistic.
- If sentiment is falling but price is rising, reduce forecast peak; sentiment may be overbought.
- Avoid forecasting 30-day trends when sentiment is volatile; use 14-day rolling average for smoother correction.
- When sentiment is high and price is rising, forecast 1–2% below true peak to avoid overshoot.
- If sentiment is low and price is falling, forecast 1–2% above true low to avoid underestimation.
